Abstract These European Resuscitation Council Guidelines 2025 Paediatric Life Support (PLS) are based on the Consensus on Science with Treatment Recommendations (CoSTR) of the International Liaison Committee on Resuscitation (ILCOR) and rapid reviews performed by the ERC Writing Group Paediatric Life Support of topics not covered by ILCOR. These Guidelines provide recommendations on the prevention of cardiac arrest, basic life support, advanced life support, resuscitation in special circumstances, post-resuscitation care, prognostication, and post-discharge care in infants, children and adolescents add brackets (aged 0–18 years), but does not cover resuscitation of the neonate at birth. The recommen- dations have been formulated for healthcare providers who take care of children and for the general public and includes recommendations on how to implement the Guidelines and system factors. Stakeholders from a range of health care settings were involved in the Guidelines devel- opment process and the views of the community advisors representing families of paediatric cardiac arrest survivors and non-survivors were also considered. Keywords: Paediatric cardiac arrest, paediatric basic life support, paediatric advanced life support, post-resuscitation care, prognosti- cation, post-discharge care, critically ill child, critically injured child

Abstract The European Resuscitation Council has produced these First Aid Guidelines based on the 2025 International Consensus on Science with Treat- ment Recommendations on First Aid of the International Liaison Committee on Resuscitation (ILCOR), reviews of the expert group composed to write these recommendations, and available selected peer-reviewed literature after discussion and agreement within this experts’ group. General topics include expectations of a first aid provider, first aid courses, contents of a first aid kit, how to approach a person with impaired responsiveness, recovery position, use of a pulse oximeter and administration of oxygen. Medical emergencies include anaphylaxis, choking, asthma, chest pain, hypoglycaemia, opioid overdose, recognition of stroke, and suicidal thoughts. Trauma-related emergencies include cervical spinal motion restriction, control of life-threatening bleeding, management of open chest wounds, concussion and preservation of an amputated body part. Environmental emergencies include drowning, hypothermia, hyperthermia and snake bite. First aid procedures for the prevention and management of life- threatening conditions that could progress to cardiac arrest, have been included. The management of cardiac arrest is described in the 2025 ERC Guidelines Basic Life Support. For commercial reproduction rights and permissions contact permissions@ersnet.org Foreign body inhalation carries potential for significant morbidity and mortality. Technological advances in imaging and flexible endoscopes have challenged the status of rigid bronchoscopy as the gold standard for inhaled foreign body management. This review of the assessment and management of inhaled foreign bodies focuses on tracheobronchial foreign bodies in children. Myths surrounding clinical assessment, use of radiography and procedures for addressing foreign bodies are sequentially deconstructed using evidence from the literature. If foreign body aspiration is suspected, prompt intervention is required to minimise sequelae of delayed diagnosis. The threshold for bronchoscopy should be low, with rigid techniques remaining the gold standard, and maintenance of these skills essential.

Their posterior teeth are still to erupt, mastication skills are immature and so is the control of respiration during crying and laughing [ 1 ]. All this creates a risk for aspiration of foreign bodies, and those aged 1–3 years are most at risk. It also occasionally happens in adolescents engaging in risk taking behaviour, adults who have learning difficulties and those who are intoxicated.

Laryngeal foreign bodies Foreign body inhalation is the fourth leading cause of accidental death in children under 3 years of age [ 2 ]. Mostly, death is due to foreign bodies that impact in the laryngeal inlet. These are typically whole grapes, boiled sweets and pieces of hot dog sausage [ 2 ], all of which are the perfect size and shape to fit in the child's larynx. Death occurs quickly, out of hospital, and management is directed towards public education about prevention and out-of-hospital resuscitation. We will not consider laryngeal foreign bodies any further in this review.

Tracheobronchial foreign bodies The median age for foreign body aspiration is 2 years, with boys being more at risk [ 3 ]. It is most common in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs), with huge numbers reported in some single centre series from Egypt (3300 children in 10 years) [ 4 ], Turkey (1887 children in 30 years) [ 5 ] and China (1428 children in 22 years) [ 6 ]. In Europe and North America, parents are well-educated about the risk of small objects [ 7 ] and there is legislation around small parts in toys. Foreign body aspiration is much less frequent as a result, meaning clinicians see fewer cases. The nature of the foreign bodies also varies with, for example, Hijab pins, melon seeds and sunflower seeds being more common in the Middle East and North Africa. In Europe, the most common foreign bodies to be inhaled are nuts, seeds, berries, corn and beans [ 3 ].

Foreign bodies cause a lot of anxiety for clinicians and families alike. Diagnosis and management can be very challenging. This review aims to explore the relevant medical literature and deconstruct myths around the management of foreign body aspiration. Myth: one can clinically exclude foreign body aspiration on history and examination The classic history is of an initial severe episode of coughing, followed by a period of clinical stability as the airway habituates to the presence of the foreign object. Children may therefore be quite settled and relatively free of symptoms at the time they present. Of course, if not removed, a foreign body may lead to respiratory deterioration over the next few hours, days or weeks. Delayed presentation may be in the form of a pneumonia that is not responsive to treatment. Eventually, permanent lung damage with bronchiectasis will occur. The main differential diagnoses are croup in the acute stage, and asthma or tracheobronchomalacia in the subacute or chronic stage.

The diagnosis is not in any doubt if the choking event is witnessed, and the nature of the foreign object is known. Even in the absence of any signs on examination or chest radiography, a witnessed choking event is a good predictor of the presence of a foreign body on bronchoscopy [ 8 – 11 ].

On examination, stridor, unilateral wheeze, unilateral reduced air entry, asymmetry of chest movement, tachypnoea and chest wall recession are all suggestive to some degree. Their presence suggests that a foreign body is genuinely there, but their absence does not exclude one [ 9 , 10 ]. Asymmetry of chest signs will only be present if the foreign object is in a main bronchus. A life-threatening tracheal foreign body can have surprisingly few clinical signs [ 12 ]. Hoarseness with stridor suggests a laryngeal foreign body.

The accuracy of clinical diagnosis has been assessed in two recent meta-analyses. Despite analysing numerous studies, no singular clinical finding was found to demonstrate both positive and negative predictive values higher than 50% [ 13 ] making their value in clinical prediction models questionable [ 14 ].

Summary In summary, any initial history indicative of a witnessed choking event with severe cough gives adequate clinical suspicion to proceed to further management for a suspected foreign body, even if all symptoms have since resolved. Similarly, any lateralising examination signs should be considered a foreign body until proven otherwise. Imaging alone cannot overrule these features (this will be covered in the next section of this review). Thus, in a stable patient, clinical assessment can give adequate suspicion to proceed to further assessment but cannot definitively exclude a foreign body.

Myth: imaging can definitively exclude a foreign body Given the acknowledged challenge with paediatric clinical assessment, a plain chest radiograph is often requested, by the emergency department, for children with suspected foreign body aspiration, particularly if it may be radio-opaque. Where a clear foreign body is seen, a lateral view is necessary to be sure the foreign body is in the airway rather than the oesophagus, but no other imaging is required before the child proceeds to bronchoscopy.

Most foreign bodies (80–96%) are comprised of organic material and are radiolucent [ 15 ]. If the foreign body is in a main bronchus, then there may be unilateral chest radiograph findings, such as air trapping, atelectasis, mediastinal shift and pulmonary infiltrate, but radiographs can be normal in 41% of children with a confirmed foreign body [ 11 ]. Suspected missed foreign bodies may be more likely to show post-obstructive sequalae. The cumulative sensitivity and specificity of an abnormal plain chest radiograph have been estimated at 81% and 30%, respectively [ 13 ]. On this basis, chest radiograph findings are suggestive enough to merit further investigation, but a normal radiograph cannot exclude a foreign body. Historically some clinicians have shown reluctance to proceed to invasive procedures even with an adequate choking history, and they use the absence of physical signs or findings on chest radiography as an indication to discharge the child after period of observation [ 16 ]. Such practice goes against consensus since a period of clinical observation achieves nothing, as evidenced by missed foreign bodies discovered months or years after their inhalation [ 16 ]

During the COVID-19 pandemic, the need to minimise aerosol-generating procedures led to many centres introducing computed tomography (CT) virtual bronchoscopy as a first-line triage tool for suspected foreign body aspiration to reduce the number of negative bronchoscopy procedures. Acquisition takes just a few seconds with modern spiral scanners, meaning that sedation or anaesthesia are not required. Sensitivity rates of 99% [ 15 ] alongside specificity rates of 98.8% [ 17 ] have been quoted, albeit often in sedated patients, making CT virtual bronchoscopy a viable way to either localise or exclude a foreign body [ 15 , 17 ]. False negatives occur in 0.5–1.2% of cases, particularly if the slices are too thick (3 mm is ideal) or there is motion artefact [ 17 ]. False positives are usually due to mucus [ 17 ]. A CT scanner is not a safe environment for a child with a deteriorating clinical condition, so CT virtual bronchoscopy is best kept for children who are clinically stable, able to tolerate CT without sedation or anaesthesia and whose clinical findings are equivocal or give low suspicion [ 17 ]. If general anaesthesia is required for imaging, such as in very young children [ 18 ], it may be more prudent to proceed directly to bronchoscopy so that any foreign body can be both identified and removed.

CT virtual bronchoscopy has a significant radiation dose, especially with thin slices. It has been estimated that there will be one additional cancer for every 4000–10 000 CT scans performed, with the authors concluding this potential risk is outweighed by the received benefit in the context of an airway foreign body [ 19 ].

Summary To summarise, all radiographic changes warrant further investigation. If the history is convincing or clinical signs are present, then a normal plain chest radiograph does not exclude a foreign body, and the child should proceed to further investigation. In the stable patient, CT virtual bronchoscopy can be an effective way to exclude a foreign body and avoid general anaesthesia, making it a good first-line triage tool. Rigid bronchoscopy, however, provides additional benefit with its ability to simultaneously secure the airway and remove the foreign body and should remain the first choice if there is any suggestion of a laryngeal foreign body or clinical instability, or if the child will not tolerate CT when awake.

Myth: advances in fibreoptic bronchoscopy remove the need for rigid bronchoscopy Fibreoptic bronchoscopy and rigid bronchoscopy are both perfectly reasonable ways to provide a thorough, magnified and well-illuminated examination of the trachea and bronchial tree, and either can be used as a diagnostic tool for a suspected foreign body.

With rigid bronchoscopy, an unstable airway can be controlled with positive pressure ventilation, and emergency manoeuvres can be performed such as manipulating a foreign body from the trachea into a bronchus to improve oxygenation. Foreign bodies can be removed using a variety of optical grasping forceps, non-optical forceps, baskets, suction and balloons as necessary. Bleeding, if extreme, can be controlled with diathermy or laser. Foreign body removal can be particularly challenging, and expertise is required.

One large series from China reported 1026 children, with a success rate of over 97% in removing the foreign body at the first attempt [ 20 ]. In that series, risk factors for difficulty were young age of the patient, foreign body 10 mm or bigger in size, distal location, and granulations due to delayed removal. The study also found that surgeon seniority was a risk factor for difficulty (presumably because senior surgeons took on the most difficult cases, but this is not elaborated upon). European Respiratory Society (ERS) guidelines advocate rigid bronchoscopy as the initial intervention of choice in those children with a positive history of foreign body aspiration and asphyxia, a radio-opaque foreign body, unilaterally diminished breath sounds or radiographic abnormalities such as unilateral hyperinflation [ 21 ].

Paediatric airway surgeons with experience in rigid bronchoscopy are not available in every hospital and, for this reason, alternatives may be required. In selected clinically stable patients with suspicion of a bronchial foreign body, delaying intervention until the daytime, or transfer to a specialist paediatric unit, did not lead to additional morbidity or mortality [ 22 ]. Fibreoptic bronchoscopy can be used to triage children who need transfer to another centre for rigid bronchoscopy, and may be used for foreign body removal if suitable equipment is available. A number of studies have suggested that fibreoptic bronchoscopy is a viable alternative (in some instances) to rigid bronchoscopy in stable patients [ 23 – 26 ], when performed by an appropriately experienced practitioner, such as a paediatric interventional pulmonologist, in a specific centre [ 27 , 28 ]. The literature reported success rate in removing foreign bodies is high (up to 90%) and complications (hypoxaemia, bleeding and mild laryngeal oedema) are uncommon [ 23 – 26 , 29 ]. Depending on the foreign body, removal with fibreoptic bronchoscopy may be laborious and technically difficult to execute. Instruments such as grasping forceps are required to be much smaller than those used with the rigid bronchoscope. For very distal foreign bodies, use of X-ray fluoroscopy of the airway, alongside fibreoptic bronchoscopy has been described for facilitating foreign body localisation, orientation and removal from subsegmental bronchi where only smaller bronchoscopes with limited working channel sizes can reach [ 30 ], with retrieval often achieved using wire baskets.

Additional novel techniques using the working channels of both the rigid and fibreoptic bronchoscopes include cryoextraction, which uses a cryogen gas to freeze and adhere to a foreign body. Although it takes technical skill and experience, this works for organic foreign bodies with a high water content and can also be used to reduce granulations and remove clots or mucus plugs [ 31 ]. Most of the literature on cryoprobe removal of foreign bodies comes from Asia where interventional fibreoptic bronchoscopy skills are more widespread. A 12 patient Chinese series and a large European series involving 16 patients showed 67% and 69% success rates, respectively, with unsuccessful cases resorting to rigid bronchoscopy amongst other equipment [ 32 , 33 ].

Inorganic foreign bodies with low water content are less easily retrieved and there are no comparative studies against other techniques to date [ 31 ]. With expertise, laser, most commonly Nd:Yag (neodymium-doped:yttrium aluminium garnet), can also be used via fibreoptic bronchoscopy or rigid bronchoscopy, to break larger objects into smaller fragments for retrieval [ 31 ].

The ERS guidelines state that whenever foreign body removal is attempted by means of fibreoptic bronchoscopy, rigid bronchoscopy should be available to manage failed attempts or acute complications [ 22 ]. Rigid bronchoscopy itself has the potential to cause trauma to the lips, teeth, pharynx, larynx and trachea. Life-threatening complications can occur in 4% of patients following rigid bronchoscopy removal and can include: immediate or delayed pneumothorax, pneumonia, tracheal laceration, bleeding and severe hypoxia. Children under 1 year of age or undergoing a prolonged procedure have the highest risk of hypoxaemia [ 34 ].

Direct comparison of the two methods is often equivocal, with calculated lower complication rates appearing to correlate to whether a series is published in a “paediatric” or “surgical” journal [ 35 , 36 ]. While respiratory complications were more frequent during fibreoptic bronchoscopy (16.3% versus 9.2%), importantly, these complications primarily involve mild severity [ 28 ]. However, there is an inherent selection bias towards unstable cases receiving rigid bronchoscopy and stable cases receiving fibreoptic bronchoscopy, which will impact data.

A recent meta-analysis comparing the two approaches uncovered significant heterogeneity, with more homogenous studies needed. However, the substantial conversion rate from fibreoptic bronchoscopy to rigid bronchoscopy implies availability of rigid bronchoscopy must be maintained [ 37 ].

This begs the obvious question: where rigid bronchoscopy is available, why proceed with fibreoptic bronchoscopy at all? Fibreoptic bronchoscopy has the advantage of allowing better visibility and access to the distal bronchial tree, so there are circumstances where a combined fibreoptic and rigid approach may be useful, but in general rigid bronchoscopy seems to be the safest option if the appropriate equipment and personnel are available.

It is worth noting that rigid bronchoscopy has a reported mortality, mostly in series from LMICs [ 38 ]. The deaths are attributable to anaesthetic problems in most cases and are ascribed to rigid rather than fibreoptic bronchoscopy simply because that is the technique they most often use. Some centres see so many suspected aspirated foreign bodies that they must triage them carefully, balancing the risk of missing a foreign body against the very real risk of general anaesthesia in their practice. In the UK, we have the luxury of considering rigid bronchoscopy under general anaesthesia a very safe procedure with minimal risk, and we can therefore set a lower threshold for intervention.

Summary To summarise, fibreoptic bronchoscopy has a role in both diagnosis and treatment in centres with adequate expertise. If unsuccessful, it is necessary to proceed to rigid bronchoscopy which may result in multiple anaesthetics, or a prolonged time under anaesthesia, both of which carry additional risk. Conversely, using rigid bronchoscopy as the first procedure provides a method for both diagnosis and treatment, whilst maintaining full airway control, and as such is considered the gold standard technique by many. Mortality varies from country to country and is often higher in LMICs. Technical and non-technical skills are crucial to both techniques and must be maintained to cover a regional paediatric airways service.

Myth: open surgery is a first-line option if rigid bronchoscopy is unsuccessful In most cases, where foreign body removal during rigid bronchoscopy is unsuccessful it is because of granulations, oedema, bleeding or hypoxia. The best option in the majority of circumstances is a multidisciplinary decision on when to stop, alongside a period of 24–48 h of medical management (steroids and antibiotics), prior to further attempts under optimised conditions. The first procedure may be undertaken out of hours; trying again during the normal working day, with a rested team and the most experienced personnel available, can make all the difference. If a foreign body is truly inaccessible to both rigid and fibreoptic bronchoscopy, thoracotomy may rarely be required. Prolonged duration of symptoms, as in cases of long-standing or missed foreign bodies, increases the risk of resective surgery, further highlighting the importance of early diagnosis and intervention [ 39 ].

Key points Legislation and parent education are crucial for primary prevention of foreign body aspiration. If foreign body aspiration is suspected, a high index of suspicion is required for diagnosis and prompt intervention is required. Where available, CT virtual bronchoscopy has a role in reducing unnecessary general anaesthesia in stable, cooperative children with a low suspicion for foreign body aspiration. The sequelae of undiagnosed foreign body aspiration are significant and lifelong, and, at least in high income countries, outweigh any risk from bronchoscopy. The threshold for proceeding to bronchoscopy should be low.

It is the authors’ opinion that it is a maxim that rigid bronchoscopy remains the gold standard for the management of suspected tracheobronchial foreign bodies in children, as it is the only instrument that facilitates airway stabilisation during diagnosis and removal. Furthermore, it is the authors’ belief that maintenance of rigid bronchoscopy as a core surgical skill is a necessity for surgeons involved in the care of children. Objective Foreign body aspiration (FBA) occurs across all age groups but predominantly affects children under three years of age. Clinical evidence suggests that tracheobronchial foreign bodies in school-age children (> 6 years) present distinct characteristics in terms of foreign body types, clinical progression, and management strategies compared to younger children. This study aimed to analyze the clinical features and outcomes of school-age children who underwent rigid bronchoscopy for suspected FBA and to propose a clinically applicable management algorithm.

Materials and methods A retrospective single-center study was conducted involving 58 patients over six years of age who underwent rigid bronchoscopy for suspected foreign body aspiration between January 2019 and December 2023. All patients underwent imaging evaluation, including low-dose computed tomography (CT) following the ALARA principle when clinically indicated.

Results The cohort included 51 males (87.9%) and 7 females (12.1%), with a mean age of 9.14 years (range: 6.17–13.83 years). The most common clinical manifestations were cough (94.8%) and wheezing (89.7%). Pen caps (43.1%) and watermelon seeds (17.2%) were the most frequently aspirated foreign bodies. Most patients (62.1%) presented within 24 h. Bronchoscopic removal was successful within 30 min in 56.9% of cases. Two patients (3.4%) required thoracotomy following unsuccessful bronchoscopic attempts.

Conclusion FBA in school-age children demonstrates distinct clinical characteristics, with non-food foreign bodies such as pen caps being predominant. Low-dose CT plays an important diagnostic role, while rigid bronchoscopy remains the primary treatment for central airway foreign bodies, and flexible bronchoscopy is useful for distal airway involvement. A structured algorithmic approach may facilitate timely diagnosis and appropriate intervention.

It remains a significant cause of morbidity and mortality in pediatric populations [ 1 ].

Most existing studies have focused on infants and toddlers, in whom aspirated foreign bodies are typically food-related, such as nuts and seeds. However, school-age children (> 6 years) represent a distinct subgroup with different behavioral patterns and risk factors. Previous studies have demonstrated that the type of aspirated foreign bodies varies across age groups and regions [ 2 ].In addition, anatomical characteristics of the pediatric airway, including narrower lumens and structural differences in bronchial orientation, may influence both the location and clinical presentation of foreign body aspiration [ 3 ]. Compared with younger children, school-age children are more likely to aspirate non-food objects, such as pen caps, due to activities such as studying and playing. Despite these differences, there is a lack of dedicated clinical studies focusing specifically on school-age children. Furthermore, the diagnostic and management strategies in this population remain incompletely defined. Therefore, the present study aimed to analyze the clinical characteristics and outcomes of school-age children with suspected FBA and to propose a practical, algorithm-based management approach.

Materials and methods A retrospective single-center study was conducted on 58 consecutive patients over six years of age who underwent rigid bronchoscopy for suspected foreign body aspiration between January 2019 and December 2023.All patients underwent initial clinical evaluation, including history taking and physical examination. Imaging studies were performed based on clinical suspicion. Chest radiography was used as an initial screening tool in patients without a clear history of choking and with no significant abnormal findings on lung auscultation.; however, due to its limited sensitivity, especially for radiolucent foreign bodies, low-dose computed tomography (CT) was performed when necessary. All CT examinations were conducted following the ALARA (As Low As Reasonably Achievable) principle to minimize radiation exposure in pediatric patients. Exclusion criteria included patients younger than 6 years old and those diagnosed with broncholiths, bronchomalacia, or bronchial tumors. All rigid bronchoscopy procedures were performed under general anesthesia in an operating room setting. Flexible bronchoscopy was selectively used in cases involving distal airway foreign bodies or residual fragments.Data collected included demographic characteristics, history of choking, clinical manifestations, imaging findings, location and type of foreign body, and details of the removal procedures.This study was approved by the Ethics Committee of the Children’s Hospital of Nanjing Medical University, and informed consent was obtained from all participants. The Institutional Review Board (IRB) approval number is B.30.2.ATA.0.01.00/428.

Results A total of 58 school-age children with suspected foreign body aspiration were included in this study. The cohort consisted of 51 males (87.9%) and 7 females (12.1%), with a mean age of 9.14 ± 1.96 years (range: 6.17–13.83 years). The most common presenting symptoms were cough (94.8%) and wheezing (89.7%), followed by dyspnea and decreased breath sounds. A definite history of choking was reported in the majority of patients, although a small proportion presented without a clear history but with suggestive clinical findings.

Regarding the type of foreign bodies, pen caps (Fig. 1 ) were the most frequently encountered (43.1%), followed by watermelon seeds (17.2%). Other foreign bodies included small plastic objects and food particles. In terms of anatomical distribution, most foreign bodies were located in the bronchial tree, with a predominance in the right bronchus.

Discussion This study highlights the distinct clinical characteristics of foreign body aspiration (FBA) in school-age children, a subgroup that has been relatively underrepresented in the literature. FBA remains a significant cause of morbidity and mortality in pediatric populations and is largely preventable [ 1 , 4 ]. Compared with younger children, who predominantly aspirate food items such as nuts and seeds, school-age children are more likely to aspirate non-food objects. This difference is likely related to behavioral factors and is consistent with previous reports indicating geographic and age-related variations in foreign body types [ 2 ].

In our cohort, pen caps were the most frequently encountered foreign bodies. From an anatomical perspective, the predominance of foreign bodies in the right bronchus observed in this study is consistent with the structural characteristics of the airway, where the right main bronchus is wider and more vertically oriented, facilitating foreign body entry [ 3 ].Delayed presentation remains a critical issue in FBA. Although most patients in our study presented within 24 h, a subset of patients had delayed diagnosis, often due to the absence of a clear choking history. Previous studies have shown that delayed presentation is associated with nonspecific symptoms and increased procedural difficulty [ 5 , 6 ], and may lead to inflammatory complications such as granuloma formation [ 7 ].Imaging plays a crucial role in the diagnosis of FBA. Chest radiography is often used as an initial screening tool due to its accessibility and low radiation exposure; however, its sensitivity is limited, especially for radiolucent foreign bodies. In contrast, computed tomography (CT) provides superior sensitivity and specificity, allowing for accurate localization of the foreign body and identification of secondary changes such as air trapping or atelectasis [ 8 , 9 ]. In this study, low-dose CT was widely utilized in accordance with the ALARA principle. Therefore, in patients without a clear history of choking but with persistent symptoms or abnormal physical findings, clinicians should maintain a high index of suspicion. In our diagnostic algorithm, if the initial chest radiography is negative, further evaluation with low-dose CT is recommended when symptoms persist or recur after a short course of medical therapy. This stepwise approach may help reduce missed diagnoses and avoid delays in management.

Bronchoscopy remains the gold standard for both diagnosis and treatment of FBA. Rigid bronchoscopy is generally preferred for foreign bodies located in the central airways due to its superior airway control and ability to remove large or impacted objects. Flexible bronchoscopy is particularly useful for foreign bodies located in distal airways and for retrieving residual fragments [ 10 ]. The complementary use of rigid and flexible bronchoscopy has been shown to improve the overall success rate of foreign body removal [ 11 ].Certain types of foreign bodies pose unique challenges. Organic materials may swell or fragment, increasing the difficulty of removal. In cases of tightly impacted foreign bodies, endoscopic removal may fail, necessitating surgical intervention.Based on our findings and previous literature, we propose an algorithmic approach for the management of suspected FBA in school-age children (Fig. 2 ). This approach integrates clinical history, imaging findings, and the anatomical location of the foreign body to guide decision-making. Prevention remains a critical component in reducing the incidence of FBA. Educational efforts targeting parents, caregivers, and school-age children are essential [ 4 ].

Fig. 2 Algorithmic approach for the management of suspected FBA in school-age children. A : Diagnostic pathway including history, physical examination, and imaging. B : Intervention pathway showing choice of rigid or flexible bronchoscopy and surgical options if removal is unsuccessful Despite these findings, this study has several limitations. It is a retrospective, single-center study with a relatively small sample size, which may limit the generalizability of the results. Previous studies have also indicated that early intervention is associated with improved outcomes [ 12 ]. Future multicenter studies are needed to further validate these findings.

Conclusion Foreign body aspiration in school-age children presents distinct clinical characteristics compared with younger populations, with a predominance of non-food foreign bodies such as pen caps. Low-dose CT plays an important role in improving diagnostic accuracy, particularly in cases with inconclusive clinical findings. Rigid bronchoscopy remains the first-line treatment for foreign bodies in central airways, while flexible bronchoscopy serves as a valuable adjunct for distal airway involvement and residual fragments. An algorithmic, location-based management strategy may facilitate timely diagnosis and appropriate intervention, ultimately improving clinical outcomes in this patient population.

Background Foreign body aspiration (FBA) is a frequent pediatric emergency with potentially serious complications. This study examines the clinical features, diagnostic challenges, and outcomes of FBA in children in the West Bank, Palestine, over 10 years, to fill a regional data gap and support improved prevention and management strategies.

Methods A retrospective cross-sectional analysis was conducted on electronic health records of 292 pediatric patients (0–18 years) from multiple tertiary hospitals in the West Bank, Palestine (Jan 2014– Jan 2024), using descriptive and inferential statistics.

Results Most cases (75%) occurred in children under 3 years of age, with males accounting for (55.8%). The most common presenting symptoms were sudden coughing (91.1%) and choking (63%). Organic foreign bodies, particularly seeds (41.1%) and nuts (10.3%), were predominant, with type significantly associated with both gender ( p < 0.001) and age group ( p < 0.001). The right main bronchus was the most frequent site of impaction (30.5%). Complications, including pneumonia (13.7%) and radiologic abnormalities, including atelectasis (17.1%), were linked to delayed presentation ( p < 0.05). Rigid bronchoscopy successfully removed foreign bodies in 92.1% of cases.

Conclusion FBA remains a notable pediatric health problem among Palestinian children. This study provides a descriptive overview of patterns of presentation, diagnosis, and management of FBA over a 10-year period and highlights gaps in hospital data recording. These findings contribute local evidence that may inform future preventive and clinical strategies. Limitations The retrospective design relies on the accuracy of electronic health records, and exclusion of cases with substantial missing data may have introduced selection bias.

Mortality is primarily attributed to hypoxic-ischemic brain injury and pulmonary hemorrhage [ 2 ]. Beyond acute complications, FBA can lead to chronic pulmonary conditions, including recurrent lower respiratory infections and bronchiectasis [ 3 ]. The condition is most common in children under 3 years of age [ 4 ], a vulnerability attributed to incomplete dentition, natural curiosity to explore objects with the mouth, fidgeting during meals, and a weakened protective laryngeal reflex [ 5 ]. The clinical presentation varies depending on the characteristics and location of the foreign object within the tracheobronchial tree, as well as the chronicity of the aspiration and imaging findings. These factors play a crucial role in guiding the selection of the appropriate techniques and methods for removing foreign bodies from the respiratory tract [ 2 ]. Rigid bronchoscope is considered the preferred method for both diagnosis and treatment [ 6 ]. While foreign objects can obstruct either the upper or the lower airway, resulting in a partial or complete blockage of the airway [ 7 ], the right main bronchus is still reported as the most frequent location of FBA [ 8 ]. The type of aspirated object varies according to age, developmental stage, and environmental exposure. Common items include food (nuts, seeds, popcorn), small toys (marbles, beads, miniature balls), household objects (buttons, coins, batteries), and miscellaneous items such as pen caps and toothpicks. Laryngotracheal aspiration occurs more commonly in infants younger than one year old due to tracheal narrowing [ 2 ].

FBA continues to be a serious public health issue in pediatrics, resulting in many emergency room visits and fatalities annually [ 9 ]. This highlights the need for more research, better education, and improved healthcare practices. In Palestine, although several centers handle cases of suspected foreign body aspiration, there’s still a noticeable gap in reported data, making it difficult to understand the true prevalence and outcomes of FBA. Regional studies provide some context: for example, a 15-year study from University Hospital in Jordan identified 103 children with FBA, including 27 deaths, with most cases occurring in boys under 3 years old, and peanuts being the most commonly aspirated object [ 10 ]. These findings suggest that Palestinian children may experience a similar burden, underlining the importance of investigating the prevalence, clinical characteristics, diagnostic methods, and complications of FBA in Palestine over the past ten years.

Materials and methods This study is a retrospective, cross-sectional analysis conducted in accordance with the STROBE guidelines. It was carried out over eight months (March–November 2024), with data collected retrospectively from electronic health records spanning 10 years (January 2014–January 2024). The study was multicenter, involving several tertiary hospitals across different cities of the Palestinian West Bank, including Nablus, Ramallah, Jenin, and Hebron, which enhances the representativeness of the findings, and a standardized data collection sheet was used to ensure consistency across records.

We included Palestinian pediatric patients (0–18 years) who were hospitalized for more than 24 h, underwent bronchoscopy during hospitalization, and had confirmed foreign body aspiration (FBA). Patients were excluded if they were older than 18, if their records contained more than 60% missing information, or if their medical files were inaccessible. The > 60% threshold was chosen to minimize information bias, as highly incomplete records could compromise the validity of analyses.

In total, 292 patients met the inclusion criteria. Background variables included age, gender, and residency, while clinical variables encompassed type of foreign body, time to presentation, site of impaction, presenting symptoms and signs, radiological findings, complications, and method of removal. Data were extracted from patient histories, clinical examination notes, radiology reports, and bronchoscopy findings.

Descriptive and inferential statistical analyses were performed using Python and SPSS. Descriptive statistics were reported as frequencies and percentages for categorical variables, and means or medians with standard deviations (SD) for continuous variables, depending on distribution. Inferential analyses were conducted using chi-square tests for categorical variables as appropriate. The study protocol was approved by the Institutional Review Board (IRB) at An-Najah National University (IRB reference number: Med.Nov 2023/3), adhered to the Declaration of Helsinki, and complied with applicable Palestinian regulations.

Results A total of 570 airway foreign body (FB) cases were screened across participating hospitals. Of these, 200 were excluded because the patients were older than 18 years, 58 due to more than 60% missing data, and 20 due to inaccessible medical records. After applying these criteria, 292 patients were included in the final analysis (Fig. 1 ). Fig. 1 Flow diagram of patient screening, exclusions, and final study population included in the analysis

Demographic characteristics The majority of cases occurred in children aged 1–3 years representing 191 cases (65.4%), while infants under 1 year accounted for 24 cases (8.2%), and 77 patients (26.4%) were older than 3 years. Boys were more frequently affected than girls, with 163 cases (55.8%) versus 129 cases (44.2%), yielding a male-to-female ratio of 1.3:1. Most children, 160 cases (54.8%) lived in urban areas, followed by 126 children lived in rural areas (43.2%) and 6 children in refugee camps (2.1%) (Table 1 ). Clinical presentation Most patients presented within 24 h of aspiration, including 180 cases, (61.6%), while 77 cases (26.4%) presented between 1 and 7 days, 21 cases (7.2%) presented between 7 and 28 days, and 14 cases (4.8%) presented after more than 28 days. The most common symptom was sudden cough presented in 266 cases (91.1%), followed by choking in 184 cases (63.0%), shortness of breath in 98 cases (33.6%), and cyanosis in 69 cases (23.6%). Less frequent symptoms included stridor in 22 cases (7.5%), wheezing in 41 cases (14.1%), and hoarseness in 20 cases (6.8%). Signs of increased respiratory effort, such as subcostal or intercostal retractions in 38 cases (13.0%) and nasal flaring in 22 cases(7.5%), were recorded as separate findings and did not always occur together. On auscultation, decreased air entry was noted in 45 patients (15.4%), while rhonchi or crepitus were documented in 8 patients (2.7%).

Radiological findings Chest X-rays were normal in 43 patients (14.7%). The most common abnormalities were radiological shadows seen in 90 cases (30.8%), hyperinflation seen in 60 cases (20.5%), atelectasis seen in 50 cases (17.1%), and pneumonia seen in 40 cases(13.7%). Less frequent findings included pneumothorax in 2 cases (0.7%) and the steeple sign only in one case (0.3%). These findings indicate that radiology alone was not sufficient for diagnosis, as a considerable proportion of children had normal imaging despite clinical suspicion.

Discussion FBA is a common, serious, and potentially life-threatening condition in children [ 11 ]. In the present study, 75% of FBA cases occurred in children under the age of 3 years. This finding aligns with the literature, which highlights the increased susceptibility of this age group, as this age group has increased vulnerability due to several factors. Immature neural mechanisms, underdeveloped chewing abilities, absence of posterior dentition, a natural tendency to explore objects orally, and behaviors such as laughing, crying, or playing during meals increase the risk of aspiration [ 12 ]. Boys were found to be more prone to FBA, with a male-to-female ratio in our study of 1.3:1, which is consistent with previous studies [ 7 , 13 ]. This could be due to greater physical activity and risk-taking behavior in boys compared to girls, although the exact reasons remain uncertain [ 13 ]. The diagnosis of foreign body aspiration involves a detailed patient history, clinical examination, imaging studies, and bronchoscopy [ 14 ]. Although a history of aspiration is commonly reported, typical symptoms include sudden coughing, wheezing, and diminished breath sounds [ 15 ]. However, some patients may be asymptomatic or exhibit symptoms ranging from mild to severe respiratory distress, necessitating careful evaluation [ 16 ]. Their clinical signs and symptoms depend on the type, location, and size of the FB, as well as the duration and degree of obstruction [ 17 ]. In our study, coughing (91%) and choking (63%) were the most frequent symptoms of FBA. Decreased breath sounds are often associated with bronchial obstruction, while cyanosis may indicate significant hypoxia—a critical emergency sign. If the foreign body remains undiagnosed, symptoms may become more insidious and mimic other conditions, such as a recurrent or persistent cough that does not resolve with standard treatments, rhonchi or crepitation indicating airway irritation or secondary infection, and fever indicating superimposed infection [ 18 – 20 ]. In our study, the interval between aspiration and extraction varied widely, with most patients (61.6%) presenting within the first 24 h. This early presentation may reflect the acute nature of symptoms in many cases, prompting caregivers to seek immediate care. Nevertheless, nearly one quarter of patients presented several days after the aspiration event, which may be attributed to delayed symptom manifestation or difficulties in establishing an accurate diagnosis. Similar diagnostic delays have been documented in previous studies, particularly in cases with subtle or nonspecific clinical presentations [ 3 ]. Late presentation, especially beyond seven days, was associated with a higher incidence of complications, most notably pneumonia and atelectasis. This association highlights the adverse effects of prolonged foreign body retention, consistent with findings reported in earlier research [ 21 ]. Pneumonia may result from persistent airway obstruction and secondary infection, while atelectasis can contribute to longer-term respiratory morbidity. In severe cases, complete airway obstruction may lead to asphyxia or death, emphasizing the clinical importance of early recognition and intervention. Overall, timely diagnosis and prompt removal remain key factors in reducing morbidity and mortality related to foreign body aspiration [ 8 , 9 ]. In this study, 14.7% of patients had normal chest X-rays, consistent with previously reported rates of 10–40%, likely reflecting the radiolucent nature of many organic foreign bodies [ 3 , 18 ]. Common abnormal findings included shadows, hyperinflation, atelectasis, and pneumonia. Despite its importance, chest radiography alone is of limited sensitivity and specificity, particularly for radiolucent objects such as nuts and seeds; therefore, the absence of radiographic abnormalities cannot exclude foreign body aspiration. When clinical suspicion is high, bronchoscopy remains the definitive diagnostic modality.

The nature of aspirated FBs varies by cultural, social, and economic factors, including dietary habits [ 7 ]. In our study, 58.9% of FBs were organic, primarily seeds (41.1%) and nuts (10.3%), reflecting local dietary patterns. Inorganic FBs, including plastic (13.7%) and metal (5.1%), were more common in older children. FBs were most frequently lodged in the right bronchial tree (30.5%), which aligns with anatomical differences that the right bronchi are wider and have a more vertical structure [ 1 ]. Rigid bronchoscopy was the gold standard for FB removal in 92.1% of cases, while flexible bronchoscopy (5.8%) was used as a supplementary method. In Palestine, rigid bronchoscopy is the main modality with a high success rate for both diagnosis and treatment, which is in line with international practice, as it is also considered the gold standard in other countries such as Turkey and India [ 6 , 8 ]. However, in contrast to high-income countries where flexible bronchoscopy is increasingly available for diagnostic and therapeutic purposes, Palestine faces unique challenges. Limited infrastructure, shortage of specialized pediatric anesthesiologists, and lack of advanced bronchoscopic equipment restrict the use of flexible modalities. In addition, difficulties in patient transfer between hospitals and lack of parental awareness, especially during emergencies or in geographically isolated areas, further complicate timely access to specialized care . These constraints highlight the urgent need to strengthen pediatric airway services in Palestine through investment in training, infrastructure, and equipment, as well as the development of clear referral pathways to ensure timely and safe management.

Beyond clinical management, prevention is fundamental to reducing the incidence and burden of FBA. Public health initiatives should prioritize educational and awareness campaigns targeting parents and caregivers, emphasizing the risks posed by small food items (such as nuts and seeds) and unsafe toys. Reinforcing safe practices in schools and kindergartens is also critical. At the policy level, the introduction of clear labeling regulations and the enforcement of safety standards for children’s products are essential preventive measures. Moreover, training first responders and healthcare professionals to recognize and manage choking episodes promptly can significantly improve outcomes. These strategies are consistent with previous studies that highlight prevention and education as key interventions for lowering morbidity and mortality associated with FBA [ 5 , 7 ].

Limitation While this study provides important insights into FBA among Palestinian children, certain limitations should be acknowledged. The retrospective design may have introduced recall bias, particularly for information obtained from patient histories; however, the use of hospital records and objective findings, such as bronchoscopy results, helps ensure the reliability of the core outcomes. Incomplete records that were excluded from the study may affect the generalizability of the findings. Additionally, fatal choking cases were not captured, which may underestimate the incidence of the most severe presentations. Conducting research in a conflict-affected, low-income setting also introduces challenges such as variable data quality and reduced accessibility to complete health records, which could influence the overall reliability and representativeness of the findings. Despite these limitations, the study offers valuable data on clinical characteristics, types of aspirated foreign bodies, and management patterns, contributing to improved understanding and future preventive strategies in this population.

Conclusions In summary, our study highlights that FBA is most frequent among Palestinian children under 3 years of age, with organic seeds being the most commonly inhaled objects. While our findings provide important insights, they should be interpreted with caution, given the retrospective cross-sectional nature of the study design. Future multicenter prospective studies are recommended to better define risk factors, optimize diagnostic pathways, and evaluate long-term outcomes.

From a policy perspective, targeted parental education and public awareness campaigns are essential to reduce preventable cases. In addition, strengthening primary care and emergency services through training healthcare providers to promptly recognize and manage suspected FBA could improve early detection and outcomes. Expanding pediatric airway services and ensuring access to appropriate bronchoscopic equipment and expertise should also be prioritized. Together, these strategies could help reduce FBA-related morbidity and mortality in Palestine. To assess the different types of management of pediatric foreign body aspirations in order to help define guidelines, depending on clinical presentation. A national survey in France was emailed to all 30 university-affiliated departments of otolaryngology-head and neck surgery and pediatric pulmonologists in France. Data concerning the center and the experience of each participant were collected in order to define an "senior expert" group with experience of extracting more than 10 foreign bodies and a "junior/non-expert" group. Both groups answered questions concerning five clinical cases of foreign body aspiration of different severities. Ninety-eight participants answered this survey (75 otolaryngologists and 23 pulmonologists), representing 28 of the 30 university-affiliated departments in France with a completion rate of 89%. Responses of the senior expert group were similar for clear-cut situations, such as an asymptomatic child with a low probability of foreign body aspiration and for a symptomatic child with respiratory distress.

However, for intermediate situations, management varied significantly according to the physician when considering clinical, radiological, and surgical management. In comparison to the senior expert group, the junior non-expert group seemed more precautious in the management of foreign body aspiration for intermediate cases, in particular, concerning the time at which extraction was performed. Conclusion: The management of foreign body aspiration depends on the physician's experience and the center's habits. In order to optimize patient care for foreign body aspiration, we suggested a management algorithm based on the senior expert group responses. What is Known: • Foreign body aspirations (FBA) are dreaded by pediatricians, pediatric otolaryngologists, and pulmonologists particularly because of the potential fatal outcome. • However, consensus concerning their management is not clearly defined in the literature.

What is New: • This study is the first to evaluate the management of foreign body aspirations (FBA) from the clinical assessment by the emergency medicine physician to the extraction of the foreign body. • A management algorithm was designed and secondarily validated by the SE group to help to emergency medicine physician and specialist to manage FBA. © 2022. With early diagnosis, the FB can be removed using bronchoscopic methods without causing irreversible damage.

METHODS: This was a single-center, retrospective observational study. Subjects diagnosed with FBA via either bronchoscopic methods and/or radiological findings, having no medical history of aspirated FB, and who were detected to have aspirated FB for longer than 30 days were included in the study. Medical records and radiological and bronchoscopic findings of the subjects were investigated from the hospital information database system.

RESULTS: Of the 255 patients with FBA, 17.6% ( N = 45) were diagnosed late. The mean age was 53 y; 28% were female, and 60% of the subjects had a history of ever smoking. The estimated residence time of the FB in the bronchial system was 22.8 months. The most common complaints were cough and shortness of breath. Forty-two percent of the aspirated FBs were organic material. FB artifact could be observed in 6.7% of posteroanterior chest radiographs and 65% of thorax computed tomography (CT) scans. Rigid bronchoscopy had been primarily preferred as therapeutic interventional procedure. It was also found that the artifact most frequently resided in the right bronchial system and was most commonly found in the right lower lobe, while granulation tissue was formed in 85% of the subjects.

CONCLUSIONS: The findings of the present study demonstrate that subjects tended to forget the FBA, leading to insidious respiratory system symptoms, with recurrent infections. In cases with an endobronchial mass lesion image on thorax CT, clinicians should consider the possibility of FBA. Tracheobronchial foreign body (FB) aspiration is an uncommon but potentially life-threatening event in adults. Symptoms typically consist of a choking event followed by cough and dyspnea, however, these findings are inconsistent and symptoms may mimic more chronic lung diseases such as asthma or chronic obstructive pulmonary disease. Chest radiography and computed tomography can provide information regarding the location and characteristics of foreign bodies and aid in diagnosis. Bronchoscopy remains the gold standard for diagnosis and management of FB aspiration. The authors describe the typical clinical presentation, diagnostic evaluation, and bronchoscopic management of foreign bodies in adult airways with a focus on bronchoscopic techniques and potential complications of FB extraction.

BACKGROUND: Foreign body aspiration is an uncommon entity in adults. Herein, we describe our experience with flexible bronchoscopy in the removal of tracheobronchial foreign bodies in adults. We also conducted a systematic review of the literature on the topic of foreign body inhalation in adults managed with flexible bronchoscopy. METHODS: The bronchoscopy database (from 1979 to 2014) was reviewed for subjects > 12 y of age with a history of foreign body aspiration managed with flexible bronchoscopy. Demographic, clinical, and bronchoscopy data were collected and analyzed. PubMed was reviewed for studies describing the use of flexible bronchoscopy for foreign body extraction in adults.

RESULTS: During the study period, a total of 25,998 flexible bronchoscopies were performed. Of these, 65 subjects (mean age of 32.8 y, 49 males) were identified who had undergone bronchoscopy for foreign body aspiration. Nonresolving pneumonia (30.6%), direct foreign body visualization (24.6%), and segmental collapse (18.4%) were the most common radiological abnormalities. Foreign bodies were identified in 49 cases during bronchoscopy and successfully removed in 45 (91.8%) subjects with no major complications. Metallic (41%) and organic (25.6%) foreign bodies were the most common. Shark-tooth (44.9%) and alligator (32.6%) were the most commonly used forceps in retrieving the foreign bodies. The systematic review yielded 18 studies (1,554 subjects with foreign body inhalation). In adults, the proportion of flexible bronchoscopy (6 studies,

354/159,074 procedures) performed for the indication of foreign bodies among the total flexible bronchoscopies was 0.24% (95% CI 0.18-0.31). The overall success of flexible bronchoscopy (18 studies, 1,185 subjects) for foreign body extraction was 89.6% (95% CI 86.1-93.2). CONCLUSIONS: Foreign body aspiration is a rare indication for flexible bronchoscopy in adults. Flexible bronchoscopy has a high success rate in removal of inhaled foreign body and can be considered the preferred initial procedure for management of airway foreign bodies in adults. All Rights Reserved. jamaotolaryngolheadnecksurg-e211548.pdf Key Points Question What is the evidence for the use of clinical predictions models in diagnosing pediatric foreign body aspiration?

Findings This systematic review and meta-analysis identified models using predictors based on clinical history, physical examination, and radiographic findings. A meta-analysis of model performance suggests that there is a potential benefit of such decision-making tools, but is overall limited because of concerns of model overfitting, inconsistent reporting of performance, and lack of model validation. Meaning Current prediction models for the diagnosing pediatric foreign body aspiration are at high risk of bias and are not recommended to guide clinical decision-making; thus, adherence to recognized guidelines for conducting and reporting modeling studies is recommended.

Importance Although various clinical prediction models (CPMs) have been described for diagnosing pediatric foreign body aspiration (FBA), to our knowledge, there is still no consensus regarding indications for bronchoscopy, the criterion standard for identifying airway foreign bodies. Objective To evaluate currently available CPMs for diagnosing FBA in children. Data Sources Performed in Ovid MEDLINE, Ovid Embase, PubMed, Web of Science, and CINAHL database with citation searching of retrieved studies.

Study Selection Prediction model derivation and validation studies for diagnosing FBA in children were included. Exclusion criteria included adult studies; studies that included variables that were not available in routine clinical practice and outcomes for FBA were not separate or extractable. Data Extraction and Synthesis We followed the Critical Appraisal and Data Extraction for Systematic Reviews of Prediction Modeling Studies and the Prediction Model Risk of Bias Assessment Tool framework. Data were pooled using a random-effects model.

Main Outcomes and Measures The primary outcome was the diagnosis of FBA as confirmed by bronchoscopy. Characteristics of CPMs and individual predictors were evaluated. The final model presentation with available measures of performance was provided by narrative synthesis. A meta-analysis of individual predictor variables and prediction models was performed.

Results After screening 4233 articles, 7 studies (0.2%; 1577 patients) were included in the final analysis. There were 6 model derivation studies and 1 validation study. Air trapping (odds ratio [OR], 8.3; 95% CI, 4.4-15.5), unilateral reduced air entry (OR, 4.8; 95% CI, 3.5-6.5), witnessed choking (OR, 3.1; 95% CI, 1.0-9.6), wheezing (OR, 2.5; 95% CI, 1.2-5.2), and suspicious findings suggestive of FBA on radiography (OR, 18.5; 95% CI, 5.0-67.7) were the most commonly used predictor variables. Model performance varied, with discrimination scores (C statistic) ranging from 0.74 to 0.88. The pooled weighted C statistic score of all models was 0.86 (95% CI, 0.80-0.92). All studies were deemed to be at high risk of bias, with overfitting of models and lack of validation as the most pertinent concerns.

Conclusions and Relevance This systematic review and meta-analysis suggests that existing CPMs for FBA in children are at a high risk of bias and have not been adequately validated. No current models can be recommended to guide clinical decision-making. Future CPM studies that adhere to recognized standards for development and validation are required.

BACKGROUND: Tracheobronchial foreign body aspiration is a classic pediatric emergency, and its associated morbidity particularly depends on the anesthetic management, which differs according to the center and the practitioner.

AIMS: The aim of this study was to evaluate the different anesthetic practices for tracheobronchial foreign body extraction. METHODS: A survey was sent via email to the member physicians of the Association des Anesthésistes Réanimateurs Pédiatriques d'Expression Française (ADARPEF). The survey included 28 questions about the organizational and anesthetic management of an evolving clinical case.

RESULTS: A total of 151 physicians responded to the survey. Only 13.2% of the respondents reported that their institution had a management protocol, and 21.7% required a computerized tomography scan before the procedure was performed for children who were asymptomatic or mildly symptomatic during the night. There were 56.3% of the respondents who reported that extraction with a rigid bronchoscope is the only procedure usually performed in their institution.

Regarding rigid bronchoscopy, 47.0% used combined intravenous-inhalation anesthesia. The objective was to maintain the child on spontaneous ventilation for 63.6% of the respondents, but anesthesia management differed according to the physician's experience. CONCLUSIONS: Our study confirms the diversity of practices concerning anesthetic for tracheobronchial foreign body extraction and found reveal differences in practice according to physician experience. © 2023 The Authors. See: https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-nc-nd/4.0 . The clinical manifestations of foreign body (FB) aspiration can range from an asymptomatic presentation to a life-threatening emergency. Patients may present with acute onset cough, chest pain, breathlessness or sub-acutely with unexplained hemoptysis, non-resolving pneumonia and at times, as an incidental finding on imaging. Patients with iatrogenic FB such as an aspirated broken tooth during difficult intubation or a broken instrument are more common scenarios in the intensive care unit (ICU). Patients with post-obstructive pneumonia with or without sepsis, or variable degree of hemoptysis often require ICU level of care and bronchoscopic interventions. Rigid bronchoscopy has traditionally been the modality of choice; however, with the innovation in instrumentation and wider availability of flexible bronchoscopes, most of the FB removal is now successfully performed using flexible bronchoscopy. Proceduralists choose instruments in accordance with their training and expertise. We describe the use of most common instruments including forceps, balloon catheters, and baskets. Role of cryoprobe and LASER in FB removal is reviewed as well. In general, larger working channel bronchoscopes are preferred; however, smaller working channel bronchoscopes may be used in situations when the patients are intubated with a smaller diameter endotracheal or tracheostomy tubes. Large size FB are removed en bloc with the grasping tool, bronchoscope, and endotracheal or tracheostomy tube, requiring preparation to safely re-establish the airway. After FB removal, bronchoscopy is re-performed to identify any residual FB, assess any injury to the airway, suction post-obstructive secretions or pus, control any active bleeding and remove granulation tissue that may be obstructing the airway. Additional interventions like balloon dilatation may be required to dislodge an impacted FB or to maintain patency of bronchial lumen. If bronchoscopic methods fail, surgery may be required for retrieval of FB in symptomatic patients or to resect suppurative or necrotizing lung process. Multidisciplinary approach involving intensivists, surgeons, and anesthesiologists is the key to optimal patient outcomes.

Keywords: Foreign body (FB) aspiration bronchoscopy intensive care pmc-status-qastatus 0 pmc-status-live yes pmc-status-embargo no pmc-status-released yes pmc-prop-open-access yes pmc-prop-olf no pmc-prop-manuscript no pmc-prop-legally-suppressed no pmc-prop-has-pdf yes pmc-prop-has-supplement yes pmc-prop-pdf-only no pmc-prop-suppress-copyright no pmc-prop-is-real-version no pmc-prop-is-scanned-article no pmc-prop-preprint no pmc-prop-in-epmc yes pmc-license-ref CC BY-NC-ND Introduction Foreign body (FB) aspiration is an uncommon but potentially life-threatening situation that requires urgent intervention. It occurs more commonly among children than in adults ( 1 ). The clinical presentation varies depending on the location of FB in the airway. Patients may be asymptomatic, but when present, symptoms range from acute onset of cough, shortness of breath and at times, asphyxiation. Patients may present sub-acutely with hemoptysis or with post obstructive pneumonia and lung abscess formation. Patients who present with acute respiratory failure and require intensive care unit (ICU) admission may have large volume hemoptysis, sepsis from post-obstructive pneumonia, or gas exchange abnormalities due to combination of significant airway obstruction and pre-existing co-morbidities. As such, these patients require timely interventions to remove the FB in order to relieve the obstruction to achieve source control.

A German laryngologist, Gustav Killian, is credited to be the first one to have removed a pork bone from a patient’s trachea using a rigid esophagoscope in 1897 ( 2 ). This opened the era of rigid bronchoscopy which became a widely used method of FB removal worldwide. Advancement in technology and introduction of flexible bronchoscopy has made it easier to achieve similar results as rigid bronchoscopy in most situations and as such, it is now the preferred approach for FB extraction ( 3 - 5 ). Even so, rigid bronchoscopy holds its utility in select situations, especially in children ( 4 ).
In this comprehensive review, we discuss the role of bronchoscopic tools and intervention techniques for FB removal in the ICU.

Clinical presentation The clinical presentation of FB aspiration varies among children and adults. Due to relatively small diameter of the tracheobronchial tree, FB gets lodged in the proximal airways in children resulting in stridor and acute respiratory distress. However, adults usually present with symptoms resulting from distal impaction of the FB. It is more common for a FB to get impacted in the right bronchial tree due to the straighter alignment of the right mainstem with trachea compared to left. Among adults, most studies show high incidence of FB aspiration in the 45–60 year age group ( 5 - 7 ). Often, adult patients have predisposing risk factors for aspiration, which may include altered mental status, alcohol or drug intoxication, neuromuscular weakness. In certain cases, FB aspiration can also be iatrogenic.

The most common presenting symptom of FB aspiration is cough, which is a primitive airway protective reflex, and is observed in 58–96% of the cases ( 8 - 11 ). Other symptoms include wheezing, dyspnea, chest pain, hemoptysis, and recurrent post-obstructive pneumonia ( 3 , 12 ). Multiple case series have reported that patients often do not recall the aspiration event and, therefore, do not report it ( 5 , 7 , 8 , 10 , 13 ). This may result in a delayed diagnosis, sometimes for months and up to many years leading to complications like obstructive emphysema due to ball-valve mechanism, bronchial stenosis, post-obstructive bronchiectasis, necrotizing pneumonia, bronchopleural and broncho-cutaneous fistulas, empyema, and osteomyelitis of the rib ( 14 - 19 ). Therefore, symptoms of non-resolving cough or recurrent bronchitis or pneumonia warrant careful clinical evaluation and FB aspiration must be considered even in patients without risk factors.

Patients with FB aspiration admitted to the ICU often, are the ones who develop life threatening airway obstruction, hemoptysis or respiratory failure. Post-obstructive necrotizing pneumonia secondary to FB aspiration may cause hypoxic respiratory failure and some patients may require ventilator support ( Figure 1 ). Rarely, patients may present post-cardiopulmonary arrest after a “choking” episode due to FB aspiration ( 20 , 21 ). In intubated patients, endotracheal tube (ETT) obstruction due to aspirated FB may result in worsening hypoxia and difficulty with oxygenation and ventilation ( 22 , 23 ). The obstruction may be secondary to an aspirated FB or iatrogenic as a result of traumatic intubation, for example, a broken tooth. It is critical to promptly recognize ETT obstruction. Activation of high-pressure alarm on the ventilator, reduced tidal volume delivered, reduced expired end-tidal CO 2 , severe hypoxemia and inability to pass the suction catheter down the ETT; all may provide clues to the intensivist ( 23 ). Diagnostic bronchoscopy is valuable in these circumstances to both diagnose the cause of obstruction and if due to FB, mechanically dislodge the FB outside the ETT into the tracheobronchial tree. The FB is then removed using the tools and techniques discussed in latter sections. Alternatively, consideration may be given to exchange of ETT especially if the FB is firmly lodged in the lumen of ETT.

Figure 1 A 46-year old man, never smoker, with history of Asthma presented with non-resolving cough and hemoptysis. He received two prior antibiotic treatments for presumed pneumonia a month apart with mild improvement. Chest imaging revealed findings concerning for necrotizing pneumonia as result of lingular obstruction (A-C). Computed tomography scans revealed high density foreign body (B) and post obstructive bronchiectasis (C). 3-dimensional reconstruction of the tracheobronchial tree was performed to localize the obstruction (D). After receiving intravenous antibiotics for 72 hours, patient was intubated electively given concern for “spill-over” of pus from relief of obstruction. A significant amount of pus was suctioned post-extraction of the foreign body (E-G). Foreign body was determined to be a corn kernel (H). Patient completed a course of antibiotics and had no symptoms on a follow up visit.

Types of aspirated foreign bodies It is important to understand the nature and type of FB aspirated as each FB has distinct characteristics and poses a unique challenge for the bronchoscopist. Also, it helps the proceduralist plan ahead with the choice of tools that may be required for its safe and successful retrieval.

Foreign bodies are broadly classified into: Organic and Inorganic ( 3 ). Organic FBs include chicken or fish bones, meat, fruit or vegetable pieces, seeds and tend to be the predominant group (47%) as reported in a literature review by Blanco Ramos et al. ( 5 ). Inorganic FBs include thumbtacks, pins, screws, coins, plastic pieces etc. Organic FBs are known to cause more complications due to their ability to absorb moisture that often result in airway obstruction and post-obstructive pneumonia. Also, they elicit a strong inflammatory reaction within the bronchial tissue, thus, making their extraction much more challenging ( 13 ). The ability to hold moisture does help when using cryoprobe for extraction of organic FB and it is tool of choice for many proceduralists ( Figure 2 ). Inorganic FBs do not possess absorbent properties, hence difficult to retrieve using cryoadhesion and require grasping tools.

Figure 2 An 80-year-old gentleman presented with acute respiratory failure requiring intubation and mechanical ventilation, a few hours after a witnessed choking episode with the first bite of a “hot-dog”. Cryotherapy extraction of the foreign body was performed and the patient was extubated the following morning. He received a short course of antibiotics to manage post-obstructive pneumonia.

Patients generally present with accidental aspiration of FB. However, aspiration may be iatrogenic which poses a different set of challenges. Iatrogenic FBs such as tooth ( Figure 3A ), dental prostheses, endoscopic capsules, broken instrument pieces ( Figure 3B ), etc., may get lodged in the airway inadvertently during invasive procedures like endotracheal intubation ( 24 , 25 ), laryngoscopy or rigid bronchoscopy ( 26 ), and administration of anesthesia ( 27 ). Timely recognition and retrieval are important to prevent any post-obstructive complications such as necrotizing pneumonia, lung abscess, hemoptysis, empyema, and resultant sepsis or respiratory failure.

Figure 3 Examples of iatrogenic foreign body aspiration. (A) A 78-year-old gentleman was emergently intubated for acute respiratory failure and a tooth was dislodged into the bronchus intermedius. Bronchoscopy was performed for hemoptysis a few days after the intubation and the diagnosis of iatrogenic foreign body impaction was made. (B) Image of a broken disposable bronchoscope (AMBU ® ) that was inadvertently introduced via “Murphy eye” of a size 8.0 endotracheal tube. This resulted in iatrogenic foreign body that required removal using a forceps. One jaw of the forceps was engaged in the lumen of the broken scope and grasped to extract in its entirety.

Diagnostic evaluation Bronchoscopy is the mainstay in diagnosis and management of FB aspiration. While it may be the only diagnostic modality in emergent situations, when patient is stable, other diagnostic testing may be performed during pre-procedural planning to reduce the complications and enhance the outcomes.

The initial diagnostic evaluation of patients with suspected FB aspiration includes obtaining a postero-anterior and lateral chest radiograph. The visibility of the aspirated FB depends on its radio-opacity, size, anatomical position in the airway and the patient’s body habitus. Organic foreign bodies like food particles and wood are generally radiolucent while inorganic ones like coins, stone particles, metals, glass pieces etc. are radiopaque. It is estimated that only around 26% of the aspirated FBs are radio-opaque and visible on chest radiographs ( 5 ). Indirect signs of FB aspiration seen on chest radiography include hyper-lucency suggesting air trapping ( Figure 4 ), atelectasis, consolidation, and mediastinal shift. Blanco Ramos et al. reported the incidence of these radiological findings from various case series as: Consolidation (43%), atelectasis (15%) and bronchiectasis (5%) though absence of these does not exclude FB aspiration ( 5 ).

Figure 4 A 13-year-old boy presented with history of whistling sound while breathing. A history of aspirating components of a plastic whistle 6 weeks back was elicited. (A) Chest X-ray demonstrates hyper-lucency of left lung with opacity (red arrow) in left hilar region. (B) Computed tomography showed a reverse C shaped artifact (yellow arrow) in left main bronchus with hyperinflation of left lung fields. A plastic whistle component was removed using sharktooth forceps that revealed significant granulation of the surrounding mucosa that was managed conservatively. Repeat bronchoscopy after 2 months showed normal lumen with mild inflammatory changes.

Computed tomography (CT) of chest helps in localizing and evaluating the nature of the FB and provides better information compared to a plain chest radiograph. The FB is visible on CT in 62% cases and helps in identifying concomitant or indicative consolidation, atelectasis, pleural effusion and bronchial wall abnormalities ( 28 ). Intra-operative ultrasonography is occasionally employed to identify sub-pleural radiolucent foreign bodies. Fluoroscopy provides real time images and is rarely used for FB evaluation ( 29 ). It has been used intra-procedurally to guide forceps especially, when the FB gets lodged distally ( 30 - 32 ).

Bronchoscopy in evaluation and management of FB aspiration Rigid bronchoscopy was introduced in 1897 for FB removal and was widely used until the advent of flexible bronchoscopy by Shigeto Ikeda in 1968. This has transformed the field of bronchoscopy including the management of FB removal ( 33 ). Flexible bronchoscopy allows better visualization of distal airways and can be performed under local anesthesia and moderate sedation though general anesthesia may be more conducive to removal of impacted FB. Overtime, with advancement in bronchoscopic tools and experience with flexible bronchoscopy, it has become the standard technique for initial evaluation and management of FB aspiration among adults ( 5 , 8 , 13 , 34 ).

The success rate of flexible bronchoscopy in retrieval of airway FBs has been studied in numerous case series. Sehgal et al. performed a large single center retrospective study including data from 25,998 flexible bronchoscopies, of which 65 were done for FB removal ( 13 ). The authors report that a FB was encountered in 49 cases, of which 45 were successfully removed with flexible bronchoscopy, an overall success rate of 92%. The authors also performed a systematic review and reported a success rate ranging between from 61% to 100%, with a pooled success rate of 89.6% ( 13 ).

While flexible bronchoscopy is the most common modality for FB removal among adults today, rigid bronchoscopy retains its utility. It is the mainstay for FB removal in children and adolescents ( 35 ). Ng et al. compared flexible and rigid bronchoscopy including factors to consider while choosing one modality versus the other in adult FB aspiration. They found that rigid bronchoscopy was preferred in patients with no comorbidities, previous failed attempt to remove FB, a longer duration of aspiration and FB of hard consistency ( 28 ) ( Figure 5 ). In the latter situation, rigid bronchoscopy is particularly preferred as rigid instruments allow better transfer and control of force in extracting hard and impacted foreign bodies. Also, it allows access to larger suction as significant bleeding may occur with manipulation during extraction of impacted FB, particularly the ones lodged in airway for longer duration.
